analysis.one_liner: Orders the Interior Department to quickly approve pending federal oil and gas drilling permits and publish permitting data.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2022 with a single cosponsor, the bill went no further than committee referral and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The DRILL Act would have ordered the Interior Department to approve every pending application to drill for oil and gas on federal land within 30 days, as long as the application was complete and met environmental and other legal requirements. It also would have required monthly public counts of drilling permits, lease nominations, and offshore survey applications; a report spelling out the cause of every permitting delay; annual staffing reports; and the handover of internal documents tied to the administration's review of federal oil and gas permitting. The fast-approval mandate was the bill's operative core; the rest was transparency and reporting [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies with drilling applications, lease nominations, or offshore survey requests pending with the federal government. The bill would have required approval of every complete, legally sufficient pending drilling permit within 30 days, and would have published monthly counts of pending and approved applications and lease nominations — a public paper trail that would spotlight and pressure any backlog [S2][S3]. Supporters argued faster federal permitting would add energy supply while prices were high, though an approved permit does not by itself produce oil or gas [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies on federal land

how_it_helps.text: Would require the Interior Department to issue all pending federal drilling permit applications that are complete and meet legal requirements within 30 days of enactment.
Would require monthly publication of the number of pending and approved expressions of interest, drilling permit applications, and offshore survey licenses, plus five years of past data.
Would require a report on every pending drilling application and offshore survey request, including the stated cause of delay, and on auctioned leases with accepted bids that have gone unissued.
Would require annual reports on agency staffing for oil, gas, coal, and renewable energy leasing and permitting.
Would compel Interior to submit all documents relating to the administration's review of federal oil and gas permitting practices under Executive Order 14008.

analysis.who_pays: Public lands, offshore waters, and the climate. The bill would have stripped the department's discretion to delay or sequence federal drilling, so decisions would move faster even where conservation or local concerns argued for care; only existing legal requirements would stand in the way [S2][S3]. The transparency reports would cost agencies staff time, and the promised price relief for consumers was indirect at best, because federal leases supply only part of U.S. energy and companies decide when to develop [S3].

drawbacks.text: The heart of the bill is a command: within 30 days of enactment, the Interior Department must issue every pending drilling application that meets the Mineral Leasing Act's requirements, taking away its ability to pace or prioritize federal drilling decisions.

For that 30-day mandate, meeting existing legal requirements is the only test — the bill adds no consideration beyond current law, so permits that clear the bar must issue regardless of broader climate or conservation concerns.

The bill requires Interior to turn over all documents and communications related to the administration's review of federal oil and gas permitting under Executive Order 14008 within 60 days, which could chill candid internal deliberation.
The promised consumer benefit is indirect at best: approving a permit does not require a company to drill, so the bill speeds paperwork without guaranteeing new production or lower energy prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions — monthly public counts of permit applications, lease nominations, and offshore survey licenses, a report explaining every delay, and annual staffing reports — are cheap and genuinely useful for anyone trying to see how the federal permitting system works. The operative mandate is blunter than that framing: it converts every complete pending permit into an automatic approval within a month, which speeds industry access to public land and offshore waters without guaranteeing more production or lower prices, since companies decide when to drill. The bill also doubles as oversight of the administration's energy policy, compelling release of internal documents on its permitting review. An honest supporter would concede the price-relief case is indirect; an honest opponent would concede the reporting requirements had merit.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and never brought up for a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Tiffany (R-WI) introduced the DRILL Act in the House on September 28, 2022, with Rep. Bruce Westerman (R-AR) as its original cosponsor.
The House referred the bill the same day to the Committee on Natural Resources and, in addition, to the Committee on Agriculture.
On October 28, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry; no hearing, markup, or vote followed for the rest of the Congress.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it, never having advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the Interior Department kept its discretion over how fast to issue federal drilling permits, and oil and gas companies ended the Congress with no new rights but no new obligations either. Supporters of slower drilling on public land got the outcome they preferred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Interior kept permitting discretion; drillers gained nothing

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill — referred to his committee as its primary committee — for any hearing, markup, or vote; it received no action there from introduction until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two supporters were Republicans — Rep. Thomas Tiffany and Rep. Bruce Westerman — and it died in committee in a Democratic-controlled House without ever reaching a floor vote, so the split was never tested in a roll call [S3][S4][S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land and offshore acreage
industries.note: The bill would have turned every complete, legally sufficient pending drilling application into a mandatory approval within 30 days, and would have published monthly permitting counts that spotlight any backlog — concrete wins for companies waiting on federal permits. Consumers might see modest relief through added supply, but the sure gains flow to drillers while public lands and offshore waters absorb faster development.
